When the Weight of Loss Changes How Everyday Life Feels

Perhaps the world around you seems to be moving forward as usual, while inside you feel weighed down by sadness, disbelief, numbness, or exhaustion.

Maybe simple everyday routines, preparing meals, answering messages, concentrating at work, or waking up to a quiet house, feel unexpectedly heavy. Waves of sorrow, anger, guilt, or yearning can arrive without warning, triggered by a song, a date on the calendar, or an ordinary moment.

You may have felt pressure, from yourself or from well-meaning people around you, to "stay strong", "keep busy", or "be feeling better by now".

Grief is a natural human response to losing someone or something deeply meaningful. It does not follow a neat timetable, and it can arise after bereavement as well as non-death losses, such as relationship breakdown, pregnancy loss, changes in health, career identity, or estrangement.

If these experiences feel familiar, you do not have to carry your grief in isolation.

With compassionate, unhurried psychological support, it is possible to have a safe space to honour what you have lost and find steadier ways to navigate life alongside it.

Could This Be What You're Experiencing?

Grief looks different from person to person, and can shift from one day, or even one hour, to the next.

You may notice that you:

  • experience intense waves of sadness, longing, anger, shock, or disbelief
  • feel emotionally numb, detached, or disconnected from people and routines around you
  • struggle to concentrate, remember details, or make everyday decisions ("grief brain")
  • experience disrupted sleep, vivid dreams, changes in appetite, or persistent physical fatigue
  • carry lingering feelings of guilt, regret, or "what if" thoughts about things said or unsaid
  • feel overwhelmed by unexpected reminders, anniversaries, milestones, or returning to work
  • notice physical tension such as heaviness in the chest, tightness in the throat, or restlessness
  • pull back from social gatherings because small talk feels exhausting or misunderstood
  • feel stuck in distress following a sudden, traumatic, or complicated loss

Grief itself is not a mental illness: it is a natural response to loss. However, when grief feels overwhelming, isolating, or intertwined with trauma, anxiety, or persistent low mood, speaking with a qualified practitioner can provide steady support.

You May Be Looking for Support Because...

Every person reaches out for grief and loss support at a different stage.

You may be seeking help because:

  • you are navigating the death of a partner, parent, child, family member, friend, or beloved companion
  • a sudden, unexpected, or traumatic loss has left you feeling shocked or unsettled
  • you are grieving a non-death loss, such as separation, fertility or pregnancy loss, health changes, or family estrangement
  • well-meaning friends or family have returned to normal routines while your grief still feels raw
  • caring for children or other family members leaves little room for your own grief
  • you have spoken with your GP about a Mental Health Treatment Plan and want a warm, supportive space to talk things through

You do not need to have everything worked out, or know what to say, before reaching out.

Understanding Grief & Loss

Why Grief Moves in Waves Rather Than Straight Lines

Contrary to popular myths about fixed "stages" of grief, real-world bereavement rarely moves neatly from sadness to acceptance. Instead, most people experience grief in shifting waves, moving back and forth between facing the pain of loss and engaging with everyday life. When loss is sudden, traumatic, or complicated by unfinished relationships, your nervous system can also remain on alert, blending grief with shock, intrusive memories, or hypervigilance.

Understanding that grief is an ongoing adaptation rather than something to "get over" helps lift self-judgment and creates space for genuine, compassionate care.

When Grief Affects Everyday Life

Grief touches emotional, cognitive, physical, and practical parts of life all at once.

Thinking, Memory, and Focus

Mental fog, forgetfulness, and difficulty concentrating are very common as the brain works to process a major change in your world.

Energy and Physical Wellbeing

Grief carries a real physical load, often showing up through deep fatigue, sleep disruption, changes in appetite, lowered immunity, or physical aches.

Emotional Shifts and Meaning

Feelings of sadness, anger, relief, guilt, or questioning your sense of direction and identity can coexist in ways that feel confusing.

Daily Routines and Responsibilities

Managing paperwork, household tasks, work expectations, or caregiving while grieving can feel overwhelming without supportive pacing.

Anniversaries and Milestones

Birthdays, holidays, and ordinary seasonal changes can bring renewed waves of emotion even months or years after a loss.

Everyone grieves in their own way and at their own pace, and support is always tailored around what feels most helpful to you right now.

When Grief Affects Relationships and Family

Navigating Loss Alongside People Who Grieve Differently

Even within the same household or family, no two people grieve in the exact same way.

One person may want to talk openly, look at photos, and share memories, while another copes by staying busy, keeping emotions private, or focusing on practical tasks. Without understanding these differences, loved ones can easily feel out of sync or misunderstood.

Over time, this can contribute to:

  • feeling lonely even within your own family or partnership
  • tension when family members have different expectations around rituals, belongings, or timelines
  • parents feeling stretched between supporting grieving children and tending to their own sorrow
  • pulling away from friendships when others seem uncomfortable talking about loss

Recognising these dynamics is not about blame: it creates room for gentler communication and shared understanding.

You Don't Have to Figure It Out Alone

Compassionate, Unhurried Support Tailored to You

Grief therapy is not about erasing memories or forcing you to move on before you are ready. It offers a respectful, confidential space where your loss is acknowledged without judgment or time limits.

Depending on your individual needs and goals, therapy may focus on:

  • having a safe, unhurried space to speak honestly about your loss and the person or chapter you miss
  • understanding the emotional, physical, and cognitive waves of grief
  • gently working through trauma, shock, guilt, or unfinished feelings surrounding the loss
  • developing practical strategies for sleep, daily routines, and managing overwhelming moments
  • navigating anniversaries, family dynamics, and returning to work or social life
  • finding meaningful ways to carry remembrance forward while gradually rebuilding daily anchors

Support is paced collaboratively with you, respecting your readiness and personal values.

What Could Change with the Right Support?

With tailored, compassionate psychological support, many people gradually find steadier footing while continuing to honour what matters to them.

Depending on your individual goals and circumstances, therapy may help you:

  • feel less alone and less pressured by expectations around how you "should" grieve
  • process painful or traumatic aspects of a loss in a safe, supported environment
  • respond to sudden waves of grief or anniversaries with practical grounding tools
  • communicate your needs and boundaries more clearly with family, friends, and workplaces
  • support steadier sleep, energy, and gentle daily routines
  • integrate loss into your life story with greater self-compassion and steadiness

Progress in grief is deeply personal, and a steady therapeutic space provides reliable support along the way.

Small Changes Can Make Everyday Life More Manageable

Gentle Everyday Steps Alongside Therapy

When you are grieving, small acts of care and realistic pacing matter far more than trying to keep up with pre-loss expectations.

Alongside professional support, many people find it helpful to:

  • allow space for waves of emotion without judging yourself for good days or harder days
  • keep daily basics simple, focusing on hydration, regular small meals, rest, and brief time outdoors
  • accept practical help from trusted friends or family with meals, errands, or household tasks
  • let people know what feels supportive right now (for example, company without needing to talk, or sharing a favourite memory)
  • create gentle personal rituals, such as writing, lighting a candle, or visiting a meaningful place, when you want to connect with remembrance
  • defer major life decisions where possible while your energy and concentration are still recovering

Strategies work best when adapted to your culture, personal beliefs, and daily circumstances.

What Could Support Look Like?

Individualised Care for Adults and Families

Because every loss and every person's support network is unique, care is tailored around your needs and preferences.

Individual Psychological Therapy

Evidence-based approaches, such as Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT), Cognitive Behavioural Therapy (CBT), Complicated Grief Therapy, Trauma-Focused approaches (where loss involved trauma), and compassionate relational counselling, may help support adjustment and emotional processing.

Family or Couples Support

Where partners or family members are navigating a shared loss together, joint sessions can support open communication and mutual understanding across different grieving styles.

Practical Routine and Transition Support

Therapy can provide steady guidance around returning to work, managing anniversaries, and rebuilding sustainable daily rhythms.

GP and Medical Support

Because significant grief can affect sleep, physical health, or overlap with persistent depression or anxiety, your General Practitioner (GP) can conduct a health check, discuss a Mental Health Treatment Plan where eligible, and explore whether broader healthcare support may be appropriate alongside psychological care.

You Don't Need to Know Where to Start

Taking the First Step at Your Own Pace

When you are grieving, even making a phone call or filling out a form can feel like a big effort.

You do not need to have everything worked out, or worry about becoming emotional, before contacting us.

At Michelle Barratt Psychology, our team listens warmly to what you feel comfortable sharing and helps connect you with an appropriate practitioner.

Whether you are:

  • navigating a recent bereavement or a loss that happened years ago
  • working through sudden, traumatic, or complicated loss
  • grieving a non-death loss such as relationship separation, health changes, or pregnancy loss
  • holding a GP Mental Health Treatment Plan and looking for a supportive fit
  • wanting in-person sessions in Brisbane or private online appointments from home

we are here to help make taking that first step calm, respectful, and manageable.

Why Clients Choose MBP

Clinically Informed Support, With You at the Centre

Michelle Barratt Psychology & Administration Services (MBP) provides a welcoming, neutral, and professionally managed entry point for individuals and families seeking psychological and allied health care.

Clinically Informed Intake

Sensitive, unhurried intake processes help us understand your circumstances and identify a suitable support pathway.

Appropriate Practitioner Matching

We connect you with clinical psychologists, general psychologists, social workers, or counsellors whose experience aligns with grief, loss, and trauma-informed care.

Coordinated Care

Where appropriate and with your consent, practitioners can liaise with your GP and other health professionals involved in your care.

Practical Referral Support

Our team assists with GP referral requirements, Mental Health Treatment Plans, and Medicare-related paperwork where applicable.

Flexible Access

In-person appointments are available at our Brisbane clinics in Toowong and Manly West, alongside secure Online Therapy / Telehealth Australia-wide where clinically appropriate.

Start with a Conversation

You Don't Have to Carry Grief Alone

You may not be sure what you need right now, or how to put words to what you have been going through.

If loss has left everyday life feeling heavier than it should and you would like a gentle, non-judgmental space to be heard, reaching out can be a helpful first step.

Tell us a little about what has been happening for you, and we will help you explore an appropriate pathway forward.

Contact Michelle Barratt Psychology on (07) 3185 0040 or reach out via our online contact form to learn more about grief, loss, and trauma therapy support.

(If you are ever in immediate danger or experiencing severe distress, please contact emergency services on 000 or reach out to Lifeline on 13 11 14 or Griefline on 1300 845 745 for confidential support.)
